Subject: On-prem K8s deployment: cluster sizing, node pools, and network checklist

Hi Linda —

Thanks again for the time yesterday. Per our discussion, attaching a short checklist we use for on-prem/private deployments to make the architecture review efficient. At a high level we want to validate cluster constraints (Kubernetes version, control plane HA), node inventory (GPU types, local NVMe vs network storage), network topology (firewalls, CIDRs, NAT/egress), and storage options for model artifacts + KV caches.

Quick asks to unblock the architecture review:
- Can you share the current approved K8s version(s) in your environment or your upgrade window?
- Inventory: number of racked servers you plan to dedicate, CPU/RAM per host, GPU model(s), and whether hosts have NVMe on-board.
- Do you have an internal image registry or air-gapped pull strategy?
- Any corporate requirements for CNI (Calico/Weave) or network policy enforcement?

We propose an initial review call this week with Diego (solutions engineer) to go over recommended node pools and constraints. Diego — I cc'd you for the deep dive. I included a short checklist (redwood_onprem_k8s_checklist.pdf) and an initial network diagram stub (network_diagram_v1.png).

Next steps: Linda, if you can drop the inventory sheet (acme_customer_inventory.xlsx) into the Drive link below or attach here, Diego will draft node pool sizing and a storage approach.

Drive link: https://drive.google.com/open?id=1a2B3c4D5

Hi Marissa —

Thanks — attaching the inventory as requested. A few clarifications from our side:
- We are currently running Kubernetes 1.25 in production and have a planned upgrade window to 1.26 in April. We prefer to keep control-plane versions within one minor of production for critical services.
- Inventory highlights (attached acme_customer_inventory.xlsx): 12 rack servers reserved; 8 x H100 GPUs (in 4 servers, 2 GPUs each), 16 x A100s (across 8 servers), remaining servers are CPU-only (48 vCPU, 256GB RAM per host). Several GPU hosts have 2 x 3.84TB NVMe each.
- We operate behind a corporate firewall with strict outbound proxies; we have an internal mirror for Docker images and can provide credentials.
- Preferred CNI: Calico with eBPF enabled; network team requires all traffic flows to be documented; we cannot open arbitrary nodePorts on the external firewall.

Open question: Do you require a dedicated control-plane hardware set, or can we run control-plane HA on the same servers with tolerations? We also have an NFS-backed SAN (NetApp) for persistent volumes — scale/perf constraints TBD.

Subject: Re: On-prem K8s deployment: cluster sizing, node pools, and network checklist

Hi Linda —

Appreciate the inventory — that helps a lot. Based on your inputs here are concrete recommendations and items to confirm before the architecture review call:

1) Kubernetes version and control plane
- Supported K8s: Redwood private deployments support 1.24 - 1.27. Given you're on 1.25 and planning 1.26, we're good. For GA deployments we'd recommend staying within a single minor version of Redwood's runtime; we can support 1.26 during a scheduled upgrade.
- Control plane: we recommend a 3-node HA control plane on dedicated control-plane hosts if you can spare them (separate from heavy GPU workers). If constrained, an alternative is control-plane on tainted master+worker mix with strict resource reservations and PodSecurity enforcement. Dedicated control-plane increases stability for evict-heavy workloads.

2) Node pools (recommended layout)
- infra/system (2-3 nodes, cpu-only, 8-16 vCPU, 32-64GB) — run logging, monitoring, ingress, Redis (if used), and small services.
- worker-gpu-inference (autoscaling) — GPU nodes for model serving. Suggested initial instance types: H100 hosts (2 gpus/node) for highest throughput models; A100 hosts for cost-sensitive models. Use K8s node labels: redwood.k8s/pool=inference, redwood.k8s/capability=gpu.
- worker-gpu-batch (optional) — cheaper A100-only pool for batch/async jobs with lower priority. Use lower QoS and tolerations.
- storage-workers (2 nodes, local NVMe) — short-lived local volumes for KV cache (high IOPS), ephemeral scratch.

Sizing heuristics (initial):
- For a model similar to GPT-3 175B served at low-latency prefixed caching, expect 1 H100 per 8-12 concurrent v1 requests depending on sequence length. We'll refine after you share qps, typical seq length, and percent streaming.
- Reserve 1.5-2GB GPU memory overhead per model-serving container for CUDA/KV cache stashing and driver overhead.

3) Storage recommendations
- Model artifacts: use networked PVs (NFS/NetApp) for durability; consider caching models on local NVMe for hot models to avoid NFS latency. Provide a k8s-sidecar that pulls model blobs to local NVMe on cold-start.
- KV cache: prefer local NVMe with a storageClass exposing local volumes (Ceph/Rook or 1:1 local-PV). If local NVMe not available, use high-performance block on SAN (SSD-backed) with write-through caching.
- PVC sizes: start with 200-500GB PVs for large model artifacts per node, adjustable per model.

4) Networking and security
- Pod CIDR: confirm with networking team; avoid overlap with on-prem corporate ranges.
- Service CIDR: set narrow range (e.g., 10.96.0.0/12) and document firewall rules.
- Required ports:
  - TCP 80/443 (ingress)
  - gRPC endpoints (often 50051 or configured port) between services
  - Node-exporter/metrics (9100), Prometheus endpoints (9090), tracing (9411)
  - Redis/TCP 6379 internal only
- Egress: Redwood needs to pull model images and optionally licensing/check-in endpoints. If fully air-gapped, we will rely on your mirrored registry and provide an offline bundle.
- CNI: Calico with eBPF is fine. We recommend network policy enforcement with default-deny and allow-lists for the inference control plane.

5) Operational considerations
- Runtime: containerd preferred. No dockerd dependency.
- GPU drivers: NVIDIA driver and CUDA stack must be installed and consistent across GPU nodes; we provide a compatibility matrix.
- Image registry: we will supply a signed list of images; if you use an internal registry we will provide pull secrets and SHA pinned images.
- Monitoring: Prometheus + Grafana, and a Redwood agent for token-level metrics and tail latency breakdowns.

Action items before the architecture review call:
- Linda: confirm whether you can dedicate 3 hosts for control-plane HA or prefer mixed topology.
- Networking: provide Pod/Service CIDR ranges and any firewall rules that cannot be changed.
- List of models to serve (names + approximate artifact sizes).

I'll draft a one-page node-pool sizing doc after the call with exact CPU/memory/GPU per pool.

Thanks — happy to hop on a 45-minute review.

Diego Fernandez
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
diego@redwood.com
